In astrophysics, the **mass loading factor** (typically denoted as $\eta$ or $\beta$) is a fundamental dimensionless parameter used to quantify the efficiency of [[galactic-outflows-and-feedback|Galactic Outflows and Feedback]]. It is formally defined as the ratio of the total mass outflow rate of gas expelled from a galaxy to its [[instantaneous-star-formation-rate|Instantaneous star formation rate]]. As a central diagnostic of the cosmic baryon cycle, the mass loading factor dictates how effectively [[stellar-and-agn-feedback|Stellar and AGN Feedback]] can eject mass from the interstellar medium and transport it into the [[circumgalactic-medium|Circumgalactic Medium]]. By regulating the gas supply available for future star formation, $\eta$ plays a critical role in controlling the growth of galaxies over cosmic time and shaping global galaxy scaling relations.

Theoretical models and cosmological simulations heavily rely on the mass loading factor to resolve the "overcooling problem"—the tendency for simulated dark matter halos to convert far too much cooling gas into stars. To reproduce the observed [[satellite-stellar-mass-functions|stellar mass function]], foundational models prescribe highly efficient, mass-loaded winds in low-mass galaxies, often requiring $\eta$ to scale inversely with the galaxy's circular velocity or the depth of its [[galactic-potential|gravitational potential well]] [Bower et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.422.2816B/abstract), [Hopkins et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.421.3522H/abstract). In this paradigm, supernova-driven winds achieve extreme efficiencies ($\eta \gg 1$) in dwarf galaxies, successfully unbinding gas. Conversely, in [[massive-galaxies|Massive galaxies]] ($M_* > 10^{10} M_\odot$), strong gravity retards stellar winds, meaning [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]] must take over to drive significant mass loading and quench star formation [Vogelsberger et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013MNRAS.436.3031V/abstract), [Schaye et al. (2014)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015MNRAS.446..521S/abstract). 

Beyond simply removing bulk mass, the mass loading factor is inextricably linked to the multiphase structure of [[galaxy-outflows|Galaxy outflows]] and the [[galaxy-chemical-enrichment-mechanisms|Galaxy chemical enrichment mechanisms]] of the universe. Comprehensive reviews of star-formation-driven winds highlight that simple biconical multiphase flow models remain robust descriptors across at least half of cosmic history [Rupke et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018Galax...6..138R/abstract). Concurrently, theoretical reviews summarize the multifaceted nature of wind launching, including the crucial roles of radiation pressure on dust and overlapping supernova remnants [Zhang et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018Galax...6..114Z/abstract). While the hot, volume-filling plasma of a wind carries the majority of the feedback energy and newly synthesized metals, observations and high-resolution models show that cooler atomic and [[molecular-winds|molecular winds]] typically dominate the total mass flux. The [[selective-galactic-winds|selective removal of gas and metals]]—governed by the interplay between the bulk mass loading and the distinct "metal loading" factor—dictates the equilibrium gas fractions within the [[equilibrium-recycling-model|Equilibrium recycling model]] and establishes the fundamental [[metallicity-distributions-and-scaling-relations|mass-metallicity relation]] of galaxies across cosmic time [Davé et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.421...98D/abstract). 

Despite its central importance in galaxy evolution theory, the exact magnitude and physical drivers of the mass loading factor remain subjects of intense active research and significant observational tension. A major open question is the "dwarf discrepancy": while large-scale simulations require extreme mass loading ($\eta \sim 10-100$) to regulate low-mass galaxies, direct empirical observations of local dwarf starbursts frequently measure highly inefficient outflows with $\eta \ll 1$. This contradiction is driving a paradigm shift, prompting theorists to explore whether galaxies are regulated primarily by "ejective" feedback (physically expelling mass) or by [[negative-feedback|"preventative" feedback]], where highly energy-loaded but poorly mass-loaded winds heat the halo to stifle future accretion. Future research aims to resolve these tensions by better understanding the microphysics of cosmic rays, the impact of runaway stars on wind thermodynamics, and the surprisingly weak outflows currently being observed in high-redshift galaxies.

## Fundamental Definition and Energetics

The mass loading factor (typically denoted as $\eta$ or $\beta$) is a fundamental dimensionless ratio used to quantify the feedback efficiency of [[galaxy-outflows|Galaxy outflows]]. It is formally defined as the ratio of the mass outflow rate, $\dot{M}_{\rm out}$, to the [[instantaneous-star-formation-rate|Instantaneous star formation rate]], $\dot{M}_*$:

$$ \eta = \frac{\dot{M}_{\rm out}}{\dot{M}_*} $$

In galaxy formation theory, the mass loading factor serves as a primary gauge for the ability of [[stellar-and-agn-feedback|Stellar and AGN Feedback]] to regulate the baryonic cycle. While $\eta$ tracks the total mass flux, the overall thermodynamics of the outflow also depend on the energy loading factor ($\eta_E$) and momentum loading factor ($\eta_p$). These related quantities normalize the kinetic and thermal energy and the momentum of the wind to the total yields provided by supernovae, stellar winds, or [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]] [Carr et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...949...21C/abstract).

To reproduce the faint end of the galaxy luminosity function and avoid excessive early star formation (the "overcooling" problem), large-scale cosmological simulations typically require highly efficient, mass-loaded winds in low-mass dark matter halos. Phenomenological models and hydrodynamic simulations frequently prescribe mass loading factors that scale inversely with circular velocity, often requiring $\eta \sim 10-100$ in the lowest-mass galaxies [Bower et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.422.2816B/abstract), [Puchwein et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013MNRAS.428.2966P/abstract).

However, empirically determining the mass loading factor is notoriously challenging due to the multiphase nature of galactic winds, and the literature currently reflects a pronounced tension between theoretical requirements and observational constraints. Direct measurements in local starburst galaxies, such as M82, indicate $\eta \approx 2-3$ in the atomic and molecular phases [Yuan et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023MNRAS.518.4084Y/abstract). In such starburst systems, most mass loading is likely confined to a thin layer in the center of the starburst where supernova explosions occur [Suchkov et al. (1996)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1996ApJ...463..528S/abstract). In contrast, recent high-resolution integral field spectroscopy of nearby dwarf starbursts has yielded highly inefficient mass loading factors as low as $\eta \approx 0.02$ [Marasco et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023A&A...670A..92M/abstract). Other differential modeling approaches at low redshift suggest $\eta \approx 0.92$, which remains more than an order of magnitude lower than the values implemented in many cosmological simulations to regulate dwarf galaxies [Kado-Fong et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...966..129K/abstract).

This discrepancy has prompted a theoretical re-evaluation of wind energetics and phase structures. High-resolution simulations of multiphase winds reveal that the bulk of the mass is often transported by cooler, slower phases, while the energy is shared largely between the warm and hot phases [Steinwandel et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...960..100S/abstract). An emerging paradigm suggests that galaxy growth may be governed less by purely ejective feedback—which requires a high $\eta$ to physically remove gas from the interstellar medium—and more by preventative feedback. In this scenario, high specific energy winds ($\eta_E \sim 0.1-1$) heat the [[circumgalactic-medium|Circumgalactic Medium]] to suppress future [[galaxy-accretion|gas accretion]], successfully regulating the galaxy even if the mass loading remains low ($\eta \sim 0.1$) [Carr et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...949...21C/abstract), [Bennett et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.543.1456B/abstract). 

Furthermore, recent theoretical models have shown that heavily mass-loaded winds radiate their energy away much more rapidly. Counter-intuitively, artificially increasing the mass loading factor can sometimes lead to *higher* [[equilibrium-star-formation-rates|equilibrium star formation rates]], because the heavily mass-loaded, cooler outflow fails to provide the necessary thermal pressure to resist the contraction of the galactic atmosphere [Voit et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240607631V/abstract), [Bennett et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.543.1456B/abstract).

Empirically constraining the mass loading factor has recently benefited from new observational and statistical methodologies. Recent techniques using starburst ages to infer wind radii have revealed that outflows typically grow to $\approx 1$ kpc within $10$ Myr while maintaining mass loading factors that exceed unity [Hayes et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023MNRAS.519L..26H/abstract). Additionally, novel statistical methods characterize the cloud-scale physics of star formation and feedback by quantifying gas-to-stellar flux ratios around emission peaks in galaxy maps to derive $\eta$ directly [Kruijssen et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.479.1866K/abstract). On the theoretical front, thermodynamic modeling reveals a complex relationship between wind energetics and central temperatures: radiative losses require highly mass-loaded winds to be driven at high central temperatures, whereas low mass-loaded winds remain efficient at lower temperatures [Bustard et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...819...29B/abstract).

## Physical Driving Mechanisms

Galactic outflows are inherently multiphase and spatially complex, driven by a combination of physical mechanisms [Hopkins et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.421.3522H/abstract), [Steinwandel et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...960..100S/abstract). The efficacy of these mechanisms dictates the mass loading factor ($\eta$), which describes the rate of mass ejection relative to the star formation rate. No single mechanism operates in isolation; rather, [[sn-feedback-model|supernova feedback]], radiation pressure, cosmic ray pressure, and [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|AGN activity]] interact to launch and sustain winds.

**Early Stellar Feedback**
Before core-collapse supernovae explode, "early" feedback mechanisms contribute heavily to the initial mass loading and destruction of star-forming regions. Photoionization and stellar winds disperse molecular clouds within $\approx 3$ Myr, well before the first supernova events [Chevance et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.509..272C/abstract). In the early phases of massive star clusters, the photoevaporation of protostellar discs from pre-main-sequence stars provides another significant mass loading source, enriching and pre-conditioning the environment for subsequent supernova shocks [Silich et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494...97S/abstract). Moreover, the mass loading and cluster wind velocity of outflows from evolving young massive clusters are highly sensitive to [[galactic-metal-abundance-gradient|metallicity]] and the evolution of cool supergiant stars, with velocities dropping significantly in sub-LMC environments [Larkin et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251006100L/abstract).

**Supernova Feedback**
The thermal and kinetic energy injected by core-collapse supernovae (SNe) is the traditional primary driver of [[galactic-outflows-and-feedback|Galactic Outflows and Feedback]] in low-mass and Milky Way-like galaxies. Expanding shock waves heat the interstellar medium to high temperatures ($T > 10^6$ K), creating overpressured bubbles that sweep up cooler, denser gas [Li et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...841..101L/abstract). Theoretical models and simulations consistently find that the resulting mass loading factor scales inversely with the galaxy circular velocity ($V_c$), typically following $\eta \propto V_c^{-1}$ to $V_c^{-2}$ [Hopkins et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.421.3522H/abstract), [Christensen et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...824...57C/abstract). The efficiency of SN-driven winds depends strongly on the [[cold-gas-surface-density|gas surface density]] ($\Sigma_{\rm gas}$) and the relative scale height of the explosions [Li et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...841..101L/abstract). There is currently an active debate regarding the role of runaway OB stars; some high-resolution models suggest they explode in lower-density environments, boosting energy loading by a factor of 5 and mass loading by an order of magnitude [Andersson et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.3328A/abstract), [Steinwandel et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023MNRAS.526.1408S/abstract), while others find their impact is negligible in dwarf galaxies due to an already porous interstellar medium [Andersson et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023MNRAS.521.2196A/abstract). Furthermore, the multiphase nature of these winds is enhanced by the hydrodynamic ablation of distributed clumps, which acts as an additional source of mass loading in adiabatic wind-blown bubbles [Pittard et al. (2001)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2001A&A...373.1043P/abstract). Ultimately, these high-energy stellar winds serve as the primary driver for launching metals far beyond the virial radius, significantly impacting [[circumgalactic-medium|Circumgalactic Medium]] enrichment levels [Suresh et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015MNRAS.448..895S/abstract).

**Radiation Pressure**
In dense, gas-rich environments—such as high-redshift starbursts and massive local galaxies—supernova thermal energy is often radiated away too efficiently to drive a wind. Here, [[radiation-driven-winds|radiation pressure]] from massive stars becomes a dominant mechanism [Hopkins et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.421.3522H/abstract). Ultraviolet photons transfer momentum to dust grains, which are collisionally coupled to the gas, driving rapid, highly mass-loaded [[molecular-winds|molecular winds]] with velocities reaching up to $800$ km s$^{-1}$ [Spilker et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018Sci...361.1016S/abstract).

**Cosmic Ray-Driven Winds**
Cosmic rays (CRs) accelerated in supernova remnants provide a non-thermal pressure gradient that yields cooler, more sustained outflows compared to the impulsive thermal shocks of SNe. Because CRs diffuse through the gas and do not suffer from catastrophic radiative cooling, they gently accelerate material into the [[circumgalactic-medium|Circumgalactic Medium]] [Salem et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2014MNRAS.437.3312S/abstract). Simulations indicate that CR-driven winds can achieve mass loading factors of $\eta \approx 0.2 - 10$ in dwarf and Milky Way-like systems [Booth et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013ApJ...777L..16B/abstract), [Kjellgren et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250202635K/abstract). The mass loading of CR-driven winds drops rapidly with virial mass, scaling as a power law with a slope between $-1$ and $-2$, and CRs are generally insufficient to drive highly mass-loaded winds beyond the virial radius in halos more massive than $10^{12} M_\odot$ [Jacob et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.475..570J/abstract).

**AGN Feedback**
In [[massive-galaxies|Massive galaxies]] (stellar masses $M_* \gtrsim 10^{10} M_\odot$), the deep gravitational potential significantly retards stellar-driven outflows. Consequently, feedback from central supermassive black holes is required to prevent overcooling and regulate star formation [Bower et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.422.2816B/abstract), [Vogelsberger et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013MNRAS.436.3031V/abstract). [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|AGN feedback]] drives massive, high-velocity winds that consist primarily of hot, diffuse gas, with a lack of cold and dense gas [Sivasankaran et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240215240S/abstract). This immense energy and volume of the hot phase ultimately causes a notable upturn in the total mass loading factor for high-mass halos ($>10^{12} M_\odot$) [Mitchell et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.3971M/abstract). To match observed galaxy scaling relations, AGN-driven winds must be highly efficient at coupling momentum and energy to the surrounding gas, although the precise loading factors remain heavily dependent on whether the AGN operates in a radiatively-driven quasar mode or a mechanically-driven radio mode [Vogelsberger et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013MNRAS.436.3031V/abstract), [Zubovas et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.479.3189Z/abstract). Direct observations of low-luminosity AGN systems like NGC 1266 reveal extremely dense winds with high electron densities, suggesting significant mass loading that may eventually lead to the outflow stalling due to radiative cooling [Lopez et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251001321L/abstract). On the largest scales, the FLAMINGO simulations show that increasing AGN feedback strength causes outflows to reach scales up to 10 times the virial radius, suppressing the gas mass power spectrum relative to matter [Ondaro-Mallea et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv241209526O/abstract).

## Scaling Relations with Galaxy Properties

The mass loading factor ($\eta$) is fundamentally linked to the depth of a galaxy's [[galactic-potential|gravitational potential well]]. Both analytic formulations and hydrodynamic simulations consistently find that $\eta$ scales inversely with galaxy mass, circular velocity ($V_c$), and velocity dispersion. In models of stellar feedback, this inverse correlation is typically parameterized as a power law, $\eta \propto V_c^{-1}$ to $V_c^{-2}$ [Hopkins et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.421.3522H/abstract), [Christensen et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...824...57C/abstract), [Jacob et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.475..570J/abstract). This steep scaling reflects the physical premise that gas is more readily accelerated beyond the local escape velocity in shallower potential wells. Consequently, $\eta$ generally exceeds unity in low-mass dwarf galaxies, ensuring efficient mass ejection, but drops below unity in massive systems ($M_* > 10^{10} M_\odot$) where strong gravity severely retards outflows [Tanner et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...899..108T/abstract), [Igarashi et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023PASJ...75.1214I/abstract). Indeed, empirical constraints from the MaNGA survey demonstrate the outflow loading factor decreasing from roughly unity at $\log(M_*/M_\odot) = 9.0$ to zero at $\log(M_*/M_\odot) = 11.0$ [Belfiore et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019MNRAS.487..456B/abstract). A feedback efficacy parameter is sometimes used to relate halo properties to galaxies, noting that galaxies with the least star formation appear to be most impacted by feedback [McGaugh et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012AJ....143...40M/abstract).

Implementing this mass dependence is essential for cosmological models to reproduce the observed [[h-i-mass-to-halo-mass-relation|stellar mass-halo mass relation]] and the faint-end slope of the galaxy [[satellite-stellar-mass-functions|stellar mass function]]. Without heavily mass-loaded winds—often requiring $\eta \approx 10$--$100$ in low-mass halos—simulations suffer from an "overcooling" problem, converting far too much gas into stars [Bower et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.422.2816B/abstract), [Puchwein et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013MNRAS.428.2966P/abstract). To properly match the evolution of the galaxy stellar mass function, theoretical models often require that mass loading factors differ significantly between starburst-driven outflows and those originating in quiescent discs [Rodrigues et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017MNRAS.466.2418R/abstract). Furthermore, these mass-dependent feedback efficiencies are reflected in the 'U'-shaped dispersion of the [[sfr-stellar-mass-correlation|star-forming main sequence]], where increased scatter at both low and high masses is attributed to stellar and [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|AGN feedback]], respectively [Davies et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019MNRAS.483.1881D/abstract). At the opposite extreme, in systems with a halo mass $> 10^{12} M_\odot$, stellar feedback is insufficient to unbind the interstellar medium. In this regime, AGN Physics becomes the dominant driver, frequently causing an upturn in the mass loading factor scaling relation [Mitchell et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.3971M/abstract).

However, as noted previously, there is a severe, unresolved empirical tension regarding these [[metallicity-distributions-and-scaling-relations|scaling relations]] at the low-mass end. While cosmological theory predicts highly efficient ejective feedback in dwarf galaxies, local observations frequently yield mass loading factors one to two orders of magnitude lower [Marasco et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023A&A...670A..92M/abstract), [Kado-Fong et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...966..129K/abstract). This "dwarf discrepancy" has accelerated the exploration of preventative feedback models, which successfully regulate low-mass galaxies by heating the halo without requiring immense mass ejection from the ISM [Carr et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...949...21C/abstract). Additionally, scaling relations evolve at high redshift; for instance, massive galaxies at $z \sim 3$ exhibit significantly higher velocity outflows (reaching up to $1500$ km s$^{-1}$) compared to typical Lyman-break galaxies, a phenomenon often linked to the onset of powerful AGN activity rather than simple stellar mass scaling [Karman et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2014A&A...565A...5K/abstract).

Beyond global kinematics, $\eta$ is also modulated by the local structural properties of the galaxy. High-resolution simulations demonstrate that mass loading is inversely correlated with the [[cold-gas-surface-density|gas surface density]] ($\Sigma_{\rm gas}$), following relations such as $\eta \propto \Sigma_{\rm gas}^{-0.61}$ [Li et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...841..101L/abstract). However, global constraints from the GAMA survey indicate that while star formation rates correlate with stellar mass, they show no additional dependence on galaxy [[lvr-relation|surface brightness]] at low redshifts [Phillipps et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023MNRAS.518.5475P/abstract). Because galactic winds are inherently multiphase, these scaling relations are not uniform across all gas temperatures. For instance, the mass loading of the warm phase tends to decrease with increasing star formation surface density, whereas the hot phase energy loading exhibits an inverted, albeit shallow, trend [Steinwandel et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...960..100S/abstract).

## Multiphase Structure and Phase-Dependent Loading

Galactic winds are inherently multiphase phenomena, comprising a complex mixture of cold molecular or atomic clouds, warm ionized gas, and a hot, volume-filling plasma. Consequently, the global mass loading factor, $\eta$, is not uniformly distributed across the outflow but is heavily partitioned among these distinct thermodynamic phases.

Observations and high-resolution hydrodynamical simulations of the multiphase ISM consistently demonstrate that the bulk of the outflowing mass is transported by the cooler gas phases, whereas the energy and metals are predominantly carried by the hot phase ($T > 3 \times 10^5$ K). In local starburst galaxies hosting [[superwinds|Superwinds]], such as M82, direct kinematic modeling of the atomic and [[molecular-winds|molecular winds]] yields a mass flux of $\approx 10 M_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$, corresponding to a mass loading factor of $\eta \approx 2-3$ in the cold phases alone [Yuan et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023MNRAS.518.4084Y/abstract). The mass flux contained within the warm ionized gas is generally comparable to or smaller than that of the cold neutral medium in these environments [Yuan et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023MNRAS.518.4084Y/abstract). In contrast, the tenuous hot phase, which fills $60\%-80\%$ of the midplane volume in simulated disks, carries the majority of the ejected energy and metals, even though it contributes significantly less to the total mass loading [Li et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...841..101L/abstract), [Steinwandel et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...960..100S/abstract).

The phase-dependent nature of galactic winds extends to their scaling relations. The mass loading factor of the warm wind phase is found to decrease with increasing star formation surface density, $\Sigma_{\rm SFR}$, while the mass loading of the hot phase remains relatively flat across different star-forming environments [Steinwandel et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...960..100S/abstract). This phase separation is also reflected in the composition of the outflow; the cold and dense gas is significantly more dust-enriched than the hot, tenuous material, which has important implications for the metal and dust enrichment of the [[circumgalactic-medium|Circumgalactic Medium]] [Kannan et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.503..336K/abstract).

The relative partitioning of mass and energy between phases is governed by the continuous interaction between the hot wind fluid and the entrained cold clouds. Prior to being swept up into galactic winds, internal feedback within giant molecular clouds determines their properties until the galactic ISM pressure becomes comparable to the internal cloud pressure [Krumholz et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2009ApJ...699..850K/abstract). Once entrained, mixing between the phases provides the primary mechanism for accelerating cold clouds, but this process simultaneously mass-loads and decelerates the hot wind [Fielding et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022ApJ...924...82F/abstract). The overall phase structure and loading efficiency are thus highly sensitive to the local galactic environment, including the ratio of the supernova scale height to the gas scale height, which is modulated by the cooling rate and the depth of the [[galactic-potential|Galactic potential]] [Vijayan et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.539.1706V/abstract).

Furthermore, the physical mechanism driving the wind strongly influences its phase distribution. While supernova-driven winds tend to generate a highly multiphase outflow with a very hot energy-carrying component, winds driven by cosmic ray pressure exhibit significantly cooler temperatures. In simulations of dwarf galaxies, cosmic ray-driven winds are found to be dominated by warm ($T \sim 10^4$ K) gas, largely lacking the extreme hot phase characteristic of violently shock-heated supernova outflows [Booth et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013ApJ...777L..16B/abstract).

## Impact on Galactic Chemical Evolution

The mass loading factor ($\eta$) is a primary driver of [[galaxy-chemical-enrichment-mechanisms|Galaxy chemical enrichment mechanisms]], dynamically regulating the metal content of the interstellar medium (ISM) and the enrichment of the [[circumgalactic-medium|Circumgalactic Medium]]. In the context of the [[equilibrium-recycling-model|Equilibrium recycling model]], galaxies are treated as continuously evolving systems where cosmic gas accretion is balanced by star formation and metal-rich outflows [Davé et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.421...98D/abstract). Within this framework, $\eta$ determines the equilibrium [[gas-fraction|Gas fraction]] and dictates the shape of the mass-metallicity relation.

A key metric in chemical evolution is the effective yield, $y_{\rm eff}$, which quantifies the observed metallicity relative to the theoretical expectation of a closed-box system. Local low-mass disk galaxies exhibit extremely low effective yields (affected by [[astration|Astration]]), which strictly requires the presence of highly efficient, metal-enriched outflows to selectively remove metals from the shallow gravitational potential well. Indeed, matching the stellar metallicities of ultra-faint dwarfs requires extreme mass loading factors in the range of $200 \lesssim \eta \lesssim 2000$ to counteract internal enrichment [Wheeler et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250703182W/abstract). Furthermore, the stellar mass dependence of the mass loading factor is the primary driver for the notably low dust-to-metal ratios observed in metal-poor dwarf galaxies, as differential mass ejection effectively removes dust along with the gas [Feldmann et al. (2014)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015MNRAS.449.3274F/abstract).

While $\eta$ is known to scale inversely with galaxy mass in the local Universe, the literature indicates significant tensions at higher redshifts. Observations of the [[metallicity-distributions-and-scaling-relations|mass-metallicity relation]] at $z > 3$ reveal that the effective oxygen abundance and yield do not increase with stellar mass, suggesting that the "simple outflow model" (which assumes standard mass-scaling relations for $\eta$) may break down in the early Universe [Mannucci et al. (2008)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2008IAUS..255..106M/abstract). Furthermore, the remarkably tight scatter of the fundamental metallicity relation—a surface connecting stellar mass, star formation rate, and metallicity—demands that the galaxy-to-galaxy variance in the mass loading factor at a fixed mass be extremely small, $\lesssim 0.1$ dex [Forbes et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2014MNRAS.443..168F/abstract).

Recent theoretical advancements emphasize that the bulk wind mass loading factor is distinct from the metal loading factor, which explicitly defines the fraction of newly synthesized metals entrained in the outflow [Zahid et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2014Ap&SS.349..873Z/abstract). High-resolution simulations demonstrate that galactic winds are subject to "differential metal loading." Because distinct nucleosynthetic sources (e.g., Type Ia supernovae, Type II supernovae, and asymptotic giant branch stars) inject metals at different scale heights, times, and specific energies, their respective yields are not ejected from the galaxy with equal efficiency. This differential entrainment can induce variations of $\approx 0.3$ dex in elemental abundance ratios within the ISM and outflowing gas [Vijayan et al. (2026)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2026arXiv260108063V/abstract). Such variations complicate the use of standard chemical diagnostics, directly impacting the interpretation of the [[o-h-radial-gradient|O/H radial gradient]], macroscopic [[abundance-gradients|Abundance gradients]], and observational constraints on the [[initial-mass-function-imf|Initial Mass Function (IMF)]]. The interpretation of these chemical yields is further complicated by evidence suggesting a variable IMF. Highly star-forming galaxies may produce proportionally more massive stars [Gunawardhana et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011MNRAS.415.1647G/abstract), while a metallicity-dependent slope for low-mass stars aligns with many observations across both dwarf and massive galaxies [Yan et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...969...95Y/abstract). These variations fundamentally alter the assumed metal and energy budgets and complicate standard interpretations of the mass loading factor.

Additionally, spatial variations in the mass loading factor within individual galaxies play a crucial role in shaping their internal chemistry. At $z \simeq 2$, gravitationally lensed galaxies display steep radial metallicity gradients that are best reproduced by models incorporating both an inward radial migration of gas and a radially varying mass loading factor, averaging $\eta \sim 2$ globally [Jones et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013ApJ...765...48J/abstract).

## Role in the Baryon Cycle and Gas Recycling

The mass loading factor, $\eta$, is a fundamental parameter governing the cosmic baryon cycle—the continuous interplay of [[galaxy-accretion|Galaxy accretion]], star formation, and feedback-driven outflows. By quantifying the efficiency with which feedback ejects interstellar medium (ISM) gas, the mass loading factor sets the boundary conditions for the [[circumgalactic-medium|Circumgalactic Medium]]. Cosmological simulations demonstrate that outflows driven by stellar feedback exhibit bimodal, minor-axis flow patterns that transport mass and metals into the halo [Mitchell et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.3971M/abstract). However, the total mass flux exiting the halo often exceeds the mass removed directly from the ISM, indicating that substantial mass entrainment occurs within the Circumgalactic Medium itself [Mitchell et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.3971M/abstract). Empirical H-$\alpha$ measurements of Circumgalactic Medium cooling rates suggest they exceed central star formation rates by factors of $4\text{--}90$, confirming the absolute necessity of efficient feedback and mass loading to prevent the excessive accumulation of cold gas [Zhang et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021ApJ...916..101Z/abstract). Direct observational support for this baryon regulation comes from DESI surveys of Mg II absorption, which provide indirect evidence that stellar feedback drives low baryon retention by allowing outflows to completely escape the dark matter halos of low-mass galaxies [Yu et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251205584Y/abstract).

A large fraction of the mass expelled into the halo is not permanently unbound. Instead, much of it is subject to gas recycling, eventually returning to the galaxy via [[galactic-fountains|Galactic fountains]] to sustain late-time star formation [Marinacci et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019MNRAS.489.4233M/abstract), [Chen et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023MNRAS.519.1899C/abstract). High-resolution simulations show that approximately half of all outflowing mass across the halo mass range $10^{9.5}\text{--}10^{12} \, M_{\odot}$ is recycled back into the galaxy [Christensen et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...824...57C/abstract). Furthermore, a fraction of the expelled gas can be recycled to form new systems entirely, such as Tidal Dwarf Galaxies [Duc et al. (2001)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2002Ap&SS.281..347D/abstract). This global recycling typically occurs on a timescale of $\sim 1 \text{ Gyr}$ and is largely independent of halo mass. Importantly, this returning gas is usually reaccreted further out in the galactic disc. The specific [[galactic-torques|angular momentum]] of stellar discs is observed to grow by factors of $20\text{--}50$ since $z \sim 2$, requiring that this accreted and recycled gas carry systematically increasing angular momentum over cosmic time to support the structural evolution of the disc [Christensen et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...824...57C/abstract), [Renzini et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.495L..42R/abstract). Theoretical models assuming an evolving, bottom-light [[initial-mass-function-imf|Initial Mass Function (IMF)]] find that such variations can significantly increase the overall gas recycle fraction, helping to resolve ongoing conflicts between observed stellar mass densities and the cosmic star formation history [Kang et al. (2010)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...713.1301K/abstract).

The role of the mass loading factor is tightly coupled to the active debate between "ejective" and "preventative" feedback mechanisms. Traditionally, theoretical models required highly efficient ejective feedback—characterized by very high mass loading factors ($\eta \gg 1$)—to physically clear the ISM and match the faint end of the galaxy stellar mass function [Bower et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.422.2816B/abstract), [Puchwein et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013MNRAS.428.2966P/abstract). However, recent analytic frameworks and hydrodynamical models suggest that galaxies may self-regulate primarily through [[negative-feedback|"preventative" feedback]]. In this regime, low mass-loaded ($\eta_M \sim 0.1\text{--}1$) but highly energy-loaded ($\eta_E \sim 0.1\text{--}1$) winds effectively heat the Circumgalactic Medium, suppressing future accretion rather than explicitly relying on the wholesale ejection of ISM mass [Carr et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...949...21C/abstract), [Bennett et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.543.1456B/abstract).

Furthermore, recent thermodynamic modeling challenges the conventional assumption that increasing the mass loading factor universally suppresses star formation. If the wind mass loading is increased at a fixed energy injection rate, the outflowing gas cools more rapidly. Consequently, a higher mass loading factor can counter-intuitively result in *higher* equilibrium star formation rates, as the galaxy must inject more supernova energy to resist the contraction of its atmospheric gas and maintain hydrostatic balance [Voit et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240607631V/abstract), [Bennett et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.543.1456B/abstract).

Ultimately, the dynamic balance of these processes shapes the cosmic star formation history. At high redshifts ($z \gtrsim 2$), galaxies generally exhibit strongly positive [[net-accretion-rates|Net accretion rates]] on both ISM and halo scales, fueling rapid growth. As galaxies evolve toward lower redshifts, the combination of progressive [[gas-depletion-and-consumption|gas depletion]] and the onset of [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|active galactic nuclei feedback]] drives the system toward a state where outflows and inflows roughly balance, slowing overall mass assembly and leading to quenching [Oren et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251023343O/abstract).

## Numerical Implementation in Simulations

In large-scale hydrodynamical simulations, the spatial resolution is typically insufficient to resolve the multiphase interstellar medium and the exact launching mechanisms of [[galactic-outflows-and-feedback|Galactic Outflows and Feedback]]. Consequently, the mass loading factor $\eta$ is frequently implemented as a prescribed parameter via sub-grid physics. These sub-grid models are heavily tuned to prevent the overcooling problem and reproduce the observed [[satellite-stellar-mass-functions|stellar mass function]].

Many cosmological models enforce an explicit scaling of the mass loading factor with the galaxy's circular velocity, $V_c$, often taking the form $\eta \propto V_c^{-1}$ to $V_c^{-2}$ for stellar feedback [Bower et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.422.2816B/abstract), [Puchwein et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013MNRAS.428.2966P/abstract). For example, in simulations using the moving-mesh code AREPO, kinetic outflows can be manually seeded with a specified mass and metal loading to simultaneously match the stellar mass content and oxygen abundances of low-mass halos [Vogelsberger et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013MNRAS.436.3031V/abstract). Other frameworks, such as the MUPPI sub-resolution model, implement supernova feedback using fully local gas properties rather than prescribing an explicit wind velocity and mass loading factor as direct inputs [Barai et al. (2014)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015MNRAS.447..266B/abstract). 

Conversely, some cosmological models avoid explicitly hard-coding the wind velocity and mass loading factor. The EAGLE project uses a thermal energy injection scheme that allows winds to develop dynamically without a predetermined speed or mass loading [Schaye et al. (2014)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015MNRAS.446..521S/abstract). By calibrating the feedback efficiency to the present-day stellar mass function, EAGLE naturally generates mass loading factors that scale roughly as $V_c^{-3/2}$ in the low-mass regime where [[stellar-feedback-and-winds|Stellar Feedback and Winds]] dominate, followed by an upturn at halo masses $>10^{12} M_\odot$ driven by [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]] [Mitchell et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.3971M/abstract).

As computational power has increased, high-resolution ISM simulations attempt to derive $\eta$ from first principles by resolving the cooling radii of individual supernova remnants and tracking local radiation pressure. In detailed isolated galaxy models, such as those employing the SMUGGLE model on a moving-mesh code, gaseous outflows are generated self-consistently with average mass loading factors of order unity [Marinacci et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019MNRAS.489.4233M/abstract). Similar high-resolution frameworks find that the emergent mass loading scales inversely with $V_c$ but exhibits a complex multiphase structure where cold, warm, and hot phases carry varying fractions of the mass, energy, and metals [Hopkins et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.421.3522H/abstract), [Steinwandel et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...960..100S/abstract).

A significant tension persists between the explicit mass loading factors required by large-scale cosmological simulations to quench dwarf galaxies and those predicted by local, high-resolution ISM models. While cosmological sub-grid recipes routinely inject winds with $\eta \sim 10-100$, resolving the multiphase ISM from first principles often naturally yields $\eta \sim 0.1-1$ [Marinacci et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019MNRAS.489.4233M/abstract), [Steinwandel et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...960..100S/abstract), which is in strong agreement with recent direct empirical observations [Kado-Fong et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...966..129K/abstract), [Marasco et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023A&A...670A..92M/abstract). As computational power increases, future sub-grid models aim to bridge this gap by transitioning toward preventative feedback schemes—heating the [[circumgalactic-medium|Circumgalactic Medium]] via high-energy, low-mass-loaded winds—to regulate simulated galaxies without artificially inflating mass ejection [Carr et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...949...21C/abstract), [Voit et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240607631V/abstract). To standardise comparisons across these varied computational approaches, researchers have developed universal fitting formulas using the Simba suite of simulations, successfully describing the resulting gas density profiles from galaxies to clusters as a function of halo mass and the specific feedback variant employed [Sorini et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024OJAp....7E.115S/abstract).

## Historical Development of Wind Theory

The historical development of galactic wind theory traces a path from simple phenomenological descriptions of galaxy formation to highly complex, multiphase models of the baryon cycle. Early theoretical frameworks were largely motivated by the necessity to explain the observed [[metallicity-distributions-and-scaling-relations|mass-metallicity relation]] of galaxies. In the classical picture, often associated with the early monolithic collapse scenario, the interstellar medium (ISM) of a galaxy is heated by supernova explosions until the thermal energy of the gas exceeds its gravitational binding energy. This mechanism was formalized in the Larson model (building upon early postulates by Mathews & Baker), which noted that massive galaxies possess deeper potential wells and thus retain their gas for a longer period, allowing them to attain higher metallicities before winds disperse the remaining ISM. Early reviews of [[galaxy-chemical-enrichment-mechanisms|metal enrichment processes]] also established that various mechanisms, including ram-pressure stripping and AGN outflows alongside galactic winds, contribute to the metal transfer from galaxies to their environments depending heavily on environmental properties [Schindler et al. (2008)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2008SSRv..134..363S/abstract).

These early formulations established the paradigm of energy-driven winds. In a purely energy-conserving scenario, where the kinetic energy of the outflow is directly proportional to the thermal energy injected by supernovae, the mass loading factor $\eta$ is expected to scale with the galaxy circular velocity $V_c$ as $\eta \propto V_c^{-2}$. As hierarchical structure formation became the standard cosmological model, theoretical models encountered the "overcooling problem," wherein too much gas cooled and formed stars in low-mass dark matter halos. To reproduce the faint end of the galaxy [[satellite-stellar-mass-functions|stellar mass function]] and prevent excess early star formation, semi-analytic models and hydrodynamic simulations universally required highly efficient, mass-loaded winds in dwarf galaxies, often explicitly enforcing energy-driven scalings to match observational constraints [Bower et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.422.2816B/abstract), [Puchwein et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013MNRAS.428.2966P/abstract).

However, the energy-driven assumption faced significant theoretical challenges. Supernova remnants in dense environments undergo severe radiative cooling, radiating away much of their thermal energy before it can perform global mechanical work. This limitation led to the widespread exploration of [[momentum-driven-feedback-mechanisms|Momentum-driven Feedback Mechanisms]]. In momentum-driven models, outflows are propelled by the radiation pressure of massive stars, supernovae, and stellar winds, transferring momentum directly to the ISM. If the outflow momentum rate is proportional to the star formation rate, the mass loading factor instead scales as $\eta \propto V_c^{-1}$ [Hopkins et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011MNRAS.417..950H/abstract), [Hopkins et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.421.3522H/abstract). Subsequent analytical and numerical models demonstrated that both mechanisms likely operate in tandem: momentum-driven feedback tends to dominate in dense, gas-rich starbursts and high-redshift galaxies, while energy-driven winds take over in lower-density environments like dwarf galaxies and Milky Way analogues [Hopkins et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.421.3522H/abstract).

In recent years, the theoretical consensus has shifted away from analytical, single-driver scaling relations toward [[multi-scale-feedback-processes|multi-scale feedback loops]] that explicitly resolve the multiphase structure of galactic winds [Steinwandel et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...960..100S/abstract). Modern high-resolution simulations reveal that outflows consist of interacting cold, warm, and hot phases, each characterized by distinct mass, energy, and metal loading factors [Fielding et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022ApJ...924...82F/abstract). Furthermore, the traditional assumption that high mass loading is solely responsible for quenching low-mass galaxies is being actively debated. Recent studies emphasize a shift toward preventative feedback, demonstrating that high energy-loading factors ($\eta_E \sim 0.1-1$), rather than extreme mass ejection, can effectively regulate star formation by heating the [[circumgalactic-medium|Circumgalactic Medium]] and stifling future gas accretion [Carr et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...949...21C/abstract). 

The classical assumption that increasing the mass loading factor strictly suppresses star formation has also been challenged; some recent equilibrium models demonstrate the counter-intuitive result that higher mass loading can sometimes require *more* star formation to balance the contraction of the galactic atmosphere [Voit et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240607631V/abstract). This rapidly evolving theoretical framework reflects the ongoing effort to reconcile classical cosmological scaling requirements with modern high-resolution observations that routinely detect inefficient outflows in local dwarf starbursts [Marasco et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023A&A...670A..92M/abstract).

## Open Questions and Future Directions

While the basic scaling relations of the mass loading factor ($\eta$) are well-established in cosmological models, the exact microphysics governing gas ejection and the empirical validation of $\eta$ across cosmic time remain highly debated. Current research is largely focused on understanding the interplay between small-scale feedback mechanisms, the thermodynamic evolution of winds, and the role of [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|active galactic nuclei]].

**The Impact of Runaway Stars**
Recent high-resolution models emphasize that the spatial distribution of supernovae significantly alters wind energetics. Runaway OB stars can travel into the low-density interstellar medium (ISM) before exploding, depositing energy in regions where radiative losses are minimized. In Milky Way-mass galaxies, the inclusion of runaway stars can boost mass loading factors by up to an order of magnitude [Andersson et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.3328A/abstract). However, the literature remains conflicting regarding their global importance. In dwarf galaxies, where the ISM is naturally more porous, runaway stars have been found to have a negligible impact on $\eta$ [Andersson et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023MNRAS.521.2196A/abstract). Nevertheless, even if the mass loading remains unaffected in these regimes, runaway stars can increase the wind's energy loading by a factor of $\approx 5$ and the metal loading by a factor of $1.5-2$ [Steinwandel et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023MNRAS.526.1408S/abstract). Fully capturing these dynamics is challenging, as the nature of galactic winds is highly sensitive to the exact scale height at which feedback occurs [Vijayan et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250200929V/abstract).

**Resolution Requirements and Wind Thermodynamics**
Simulating the multiphase nature of winds imposes stringent resolution requirements on hydrodynamic simulations. Traditional cosmological models often fail to resolve the cooling lengths of outflowing gas. Recent work demonstrates that adaptively refining the simulation grid to resolve the local cooling length (down to $\approx 18$ pc) in the inner [[circumgalactic-medium|Circumgalactic Medium]] systematically alters wind energetics [Rey et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024MNRAS.528.5412R/abstract). Better-resolved outflows remain hotter for longer as they propagate outwards, which boosts the time-averaged mass loading factor by a factor of 2 and the energy loading by a factor of 5. These findings imply that numerical overcooling in under-resolved simulations may lead to artificial suppression of outflow efficiencies.

**High-Redshift Outflows**
Direct observations of high-redshift outflows using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) have introduced new tensions into the theoretical consensus. While cosmological models typically require $\eta \gg 1$ in low-mass halos to prevent overcooling, empirical constraints suggest that standard mass-loaded outflow models fail to reproduce observed oxygen yields at $z > 3$ [Mannucci et al. (2008)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2008IAUS..255..106M/abstract). Recent JWST analyses of galaxies at $z=3-10$ indicate that matching the observed [[metallicity-distributions-and-scaling-relations|mass-metallicity relation]] actually requires surprisingly weak outflows, with mass loading factors as low as $\eta \approx 0.25$ [Pallottini et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240800061P/abstract). Furthermore, comparison between JWST observations and models indicates that matching stellar mass growth in the first galaxies ($z=6-12$) requires feedback efficiencies roughly three times lower than those prescribed in later-universe models [Dressler et al. (2026)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2026arXiv260201549D/abstract). Adding to the complexity, supermassive black holes in the early Universe may have transitioned from providing [[positive-feedback-astrophysics|Positive feedback (astrophysics)]] that stimulated star formation at $z > 6$ to driving energy-conserving outflows that eventually quenched it [Silk et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...961L..39S/abstract).

**AGN Coupling Efficiency**
In massive galaxies ($M_* > 10^{10} M_\odot$), Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics dominates gas ejection. While the transition from stellar to AGN-driven winds is well-established, the exact AGN coupling efficiency ($f_{\rm AGN}$) and momentum loading required to drive these macroscopic outflows remain actively debated [Zubovas et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.479.3189Z/abstract). Recent efforts have turned to multi-messenger astrophysics to constrain the baryon loading factor of AGN jets. By analyzing the diffuse gamma-ray and neutrino fluxes generated by cosmic-ray interactions in the intracluster medium, researchers have placed strict upper limits on the efficiency with which gravitational energy is converted into relativistic hadronic particles, finding $\eta_{p, \rm grav} \lesssim 2 \times 10^{-3} - 0.1$ [Shi et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022ApJ...927...33S/abstract), [Shi et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...957..101S/abstract). Determining how this microscopic coupling translates to the macroscopic mass loading of the host galaxy's ISM remains a critical frontier in feedback physics.

**Dwarf Galaxy Feedback Constraints**
Observational constraints on stellar feedback in dwarf galaxies remain a priority, as it is recognized that feedback in these low-mass systems directly impacts critical properties such as their inner dark matter densities and reionization histories [Collins et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022NatAs...6..647C/abstract).

**Kinematical Fluctuations**
Another emerging question involves the inherent dynamics of the stars and gas. Recent studies have discovered an inverse log-linear relation between kinematical fluctuations and galaxy stellar surface mass densities, suggesting an inherent asymmetry in stellar motion that may be coupled to internal feedback and mass transport mechanisms [Zhong et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...957L..12Z/abstract).
